title: Tenses
tagline: Grammar · time and aspect, choosing the right verb form

sourceNote.boardprep: All rules, tables, example sentences, questions and answers on this page are original BoardPrep material written for practice and are not taken from any textbook, guide or past paper.

overview.intro: A tense tells the reader when something happens and whether the action is complete, continuing or repeated. Most tense errors come from a small set of causes: ignoring time words such as since, yesterday or by next month, mixing tenses inside one sentence, and using continuous forms with verbs that do not take them. This chapter gives you the twelve forms, the rules for choosing between them and a method for checking your own sentences.

facts.label: Main idea
facts.value: The verb form must match the time and the aspect of the action

facts.label: Four aspects
facts.value: Simple, continuous, perfect and perfect continuous

facts.label: Biggest clue
facts.value: Time words such as since, for, ago, yesterday, by then and already

facts.label: Best habit
facts.value: Underline the time word first, then choose the form

learn.title: The core idea: time plus aspect

blocks.text: Every English tense answers two questions. First, when: present, past or future? Second, in what way: as a plain fact or event (simple), as something in progress (continuous), as something completed before a chosen point (perfect), or as something in progress over a stretch of time up to that point (perfect continuous)? Three times multiplied by four aspects gives twelve forms.

items.meaning: Base verb (add s or es with he, she, it). Habits, permanent facts, universal truths, timetables. Example: The bus leaves at seven.
am, is or are plus the -ing form. Actions happening now, temporary situations, firm future plans. Example: The children are drawing.
has or have plus the past participle. A past action linked to the present, or an experience at an unstated time. Example: She has finished her project.
has or have been plus the -ing form. An action that began in the past and is still going on, or has only just stopped. Example: It has been raining since noon.
The past form of the verb. A finished action at a definite time in the past. Example: We visited the fort last winter.
was or were plus the -ing form. An action in progress at a past moment, often interrupted. Example: I was reading when the bell rang.
had plus the past participle. The earlier of two past actions. Example: The film had begun before we found our seats.
had been plus the -ing form. An action that had been going on up to a past moment. Example: They had been waiting for an hour when the train came.
will (or shall with I and we) plus the base verb. Decisions, predictions and promises. Example: I shall call you tonight.
will be plus the -ing form. An action that will be in progress at a future moment. Example: This time tomorrow I shall be flying to Chennai.
will have plus the past participle. An action that will be complete by a future time. Example: By June she will have finished the course.
will have been plus the -ing form. Duration up to a future point. Example: By May he will have been teaching here for ten years.

items: Rule 1. Universal truths and scientific facts take the simple present, whatever the tense of the rest of the sentence: The teacher explained that water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level.
Rule 2. Since and for go with the present perfect (or present perfect continuous). Since names a starting point (since 2019, since Monday); for names a length of time (for six years, for an hour).
Rule 3. A definite past time word such as yesterday, last week, ago or in 1998 needs the simple past, not the present perfect: She left an hour ago, not She has left an hour ago.
Rule 4. When two past actions happen in sequence, the earlier one is in the past perfect and the later one in the simple past: When I reached the station, the train had left.
Rule 5. In clauses of time and condition that refer to the future (after when, before, as soon as, until, if), use the present tense, not will: I shall call you when I reach home.

Rule 6. Verbs of state, thought, feeling and possession (know, believe, like, love, want, need, belong, seem, understand, own) are not normally used in continuous forms. Say I know the answer, not I am knowing the answer.
Rule 7. Keep tenses consistent within a narrative. Change tense only when the time really changes.

items.text: The sun ___ (rise) in the east. Answer: rises.
items.note: A fact that is always true: simple present.

items.text: Listen! Someone ___ (knock) at the door. Answer: is knocking.
items.note: Listen and Look signal an action happening now: present continuous.

items.text: We ___ (live) in this town since 2015. Answer: have lived (or have been living).
items.note: Since needs a perfect form. Both are acceptable; the continuous form stresses the continuing period.

items.text: When the inspector arrived, the manager ___ (leave) already. Answer: had left.
items.note: Leaving happened first, so past perfect.

items.text: I ___ (walk) home when it started to pour. Answer: was walking.
items.note: A longer action in progress interrupted by a shorter one: past continuous plus simple past.

items.text: By the time you read this letter, I ___ (reach) Kolkata. Answer: shall have reached.
items.note: Complete before a future point: future perfect. Will have reached is also acceptable with I in modern usage.

items.text: They ___ (practise) for two hours when the coach finally arrived. Answer: had been practising.
items.note: Duration up to a past moment: past perfect continuous.

items.text: If she ___ (work) hard, she will pass. Answer: works.
items.note: Present tense in the if clause, will in the main clause.

learn.title: Common mistakes and how to correct them

items.text: Wrong: I am waiting here since nine o'clock. Right: I have been waiting here since nine o'clock.
items.note: Since with a continuing action needs a perfect form.

items.text: Wrong: He has gone to the market yesterday. Right: He went to the market yesterday.
items.note: Yesterday is a definite past time, so use the simple past.

items.text: Wrong: I am knowing his brother. Right: I know his brother.
items.note: Know is a verb of state and is not used in the continuous.

items.text: Wrong: When she will come, tell her the news. Right: When she comes, tell her the news.
items.note: No will in a time clause about the future.

items.text: Wrong: Before I reached, the show started. Right: Before I reached, the show had started.
items.note: The show started earlier than my arrival; use the past perfect.

items.text: Wrong: The teacher said that the earth was round. Better: The teacher said that the earth is round.
items.note: A universal truth stays in the simple present. Using the past here is a common slip.

items: Step 1. Read the whole sentence, not just the gap. Decide who is acting and what the time is.
Step 2. Underline time signals: since, for, ago, yesterday, already, just, yet, by then, before, after, when.
Step 3. If two actions are linked, decide which came first. The earlier one usually needs a perfect form.
Step 4. Check whether the verb is a stative verb. If it is, avoid the continuous.
Step 5. Check subject-verb agreement in the form you choose (she has, they have).
Step 6. Read the completed sentence aloud in your head. If it sounds odd, recheck the time word.
When more than one form is acceptable, write the one that fits best, and do not change tense within the sentence without a reason.

keyPoints: Twelve tense forms come from three times (present, past, future) and four aspects (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous).
Since names a starting point and for names a duration; both need a perfect form when the action continues to now.
A definite past time word (yesterday, ago, last year) requires the simple past.
The earlier of two past actions takes the past perfect; the later takes the simple past.
Time and condition clauses about the future use the present tense, not will.
Verbs of state (know, like, want, belong, seem) are not normally used in the continuous.
Universal truths stay in the simple present even in reported statements.
Underline the time word first, then choose the form.
examFocus: Filling gaps with the correct form of the verb given in brackets.
Spotting and correcting tense errors in a sentence or short passage.
Rewriting a sentence in a different tense while keeping the meaning.
Using since, for, ago, already, yet and just correctly.
Keeping tenses consistent in a paragraph or a narrative.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct option: By the time the guests arrived, we ___ the food.
questions.explanation: Cooking was completed before the guests arrived, so the earlier action takes the past perfect.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the simple past or present perfect for the earlier of two past actions.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct option: The sun ___ in the east.
questions.explanation: A fact that is always true is expressed in the simple present.
questions.commonMistake: Using the present continuous because the sun seems to be moving.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct option: My cousin has lived in Pune ___ 2019.
questions.explanation: 2019 is a starting point in time, so since is used. For would be used with a length of time such as five years.
questions.commonMistake: Using for with a point in time.

questions.prompt: Which of these sentences is grammatically correct?
options: I am knowing the answer to this question.
I know the answer to this question.
I have been knowing the answer to this question.
I was knowing the answer to this question.
questions.answer: I know the answer to this question.
questions.explanation: Know is a verb of state and is not normally used in continuous forms.
questions.commonMistake: Adding -ing to verbs such as know, want, like and believe.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank with the correct form of the verb: Look! The children ___ (play) in the rain.
questions.explanation: Look signals an action happening at this moment, so the present continuous is used.
questions.commonMistake: Writing play, which is the simple present, for a scene happening now.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank with the correct form of the verb: If it ___ (rain) tomorrow, the match will be cancelled.
questions.explanation: In an if clause about the future, the simple present is used and will is kept for the main clause.
questions.commonMistake: Writing will rain in the if clause.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank with the correct form of the verb: By next June, my sister ___ (complete) her course.
questions.explanation: The action will be finished before a future point in time (next June), which needs the future perfect. Shall have completed is possible only with I or we.
questions.commonMistake: Using will complete, which does not show that the action is finished by then.

questions.prompt: Correct the sentence by changing the verb form: He is working in this office since 2015.
questions.answer: He has been working in this office since 2015.
questions.explanation: Since with an action that started in the past and continues now needs the present perfect continuous. He has worked in this office since 2015 is also acceptable.
questions.commonMistake: Keeping the present continuous with since.

questions.prompt: Join the two sentences into one, using after and the past perfect: Ravi finished his homework. Then he went out to play.
questions.answer: After Ravi had finished his homework, he went out to play.
questions.explanation: The earlier action (finishing) takes the past perfect and the later action takes the simple past. The order can be reversed: Ravi went out to play after he had finished his homework.
questions.commonMistake: Using the simple past in both clauses. It is often accepted in speech, but the past perfect shows the sequence clearly.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between the simple past and the present perfect. Give one example of each.
questions.answer: The simple past is used for an action that finished at a definite time in the past, and that time is usually stated or understood: We visited the museum last Sunday. The present perfect is used for a past action that is connected with the present, or for an experience at an unstated time: We have visited the museum twice. The present perfect is not used with a definite past time word such as yesterday or last Sunday.
questions.explanation: Give the rule for each tense, one correct example each and, for full credit, the point about definite time words.
questions.commonMistake: Writing I have seen him yesterday.

questions.prompt: Each sentence contains one tense error. Rewrite it correctly. (a) She has left for Delhi yesterday. (b) When I reached, the train already left. (c) He will call you when he will reach home. (d) I am waiting here since nine o'clock.
questions.answer: (a) She left for Delhi yesterday. (b) When I reached, the train had already left. (c) He will call you when he reaches home. (d) I have been waiting here since nine o'clock.
questions.explanation: (a) Yesterday is a definite past time, so the simple past is needed. (b) The leaving came before the arrival, so use the past perfect. (c) A time clause about the future takes the present tense. (d) Since with a continuing action needs the present perfect continuous.
questions.commonMistake: Correcting the verb but leaving the time word in conflict with the tense.

questions.prompt: Name the tense of the verb in each sentence: (a) They had been practising for an hour. (b) The bell will have rung by then. (c) I shall be travelling tomorrow. (d) Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level.
questions.answer: (a) Past perfect continuous. (b) Future perfect. (c) Future continuous. (d) Simple present.
questions.explanation: (a) had been plus -ing. (b) will have plus past participle. (c) shall be plus -ing. (d) A universal truth in the simple present.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing the past perfect continuous with the present perfect continuous. Look at had or have.
